analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA from ever regulating coal ash as hazardous waste.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee at the end of the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the nation's waste law to permanently exempt fly ash, bottom ash, slag, and other coal combustion waste from being regulated as hazardous material. That would block the EPA's option to set hazardous-waste rules for coal ash storage and disposal, leaving power plants free to handle the material under looser standards. Communities living near ash ponds would continue to bear the risk of contaminated groundwater from unlined or leaking disposal sites.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal-burning electric utilities gain the most: they would avoid the disposal, lining, and monitoring costs that come with a hazardous-waste designation, costs that might otherwise be passed to electricity customers. Companies that sell or recycle fly ash for products like concrete would also benefit, because a hazardous label can depress demand for reused ash.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Solid Waste Disposal Act so that fly ash, bottom ash, slag, and flue gas control waste from coal combustion 'shall not be subject to regulation' as hazardous waste under subtitle C [S3].
The CRS summary confirms the bill exempts these coal combustion byproducts from hazardous-waste regulation under the Act [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People living near coal ash ponds and landfills would keep facing the risk of contaminated drinking water and soil, since the bill forecloses the strictest federal disposal standards. Taxpayers and neighboring communities can also be left holding cleanup costs when unregulated sites fail, as downstream litigation and Superfund-style cleanups often show.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near coal ash disposal sites

drawbacks.text: A blanket exemption forecloses the strictest federal standards for material that contains arsenic, mercury, and lead, leaving storage and disposal largely to state rules of varying strength.

Good-faith objection: a hazardous-waste designation could have imposed large compliance costs on utilities and reduced the market for recycling fly ash into concrete and other construction materials, with some costs likely passed to electricity customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit flows to a single industry: cheaper disposal of combustion waste. The cost is a permanent bar on the strongest federal protections for waste that can leach toxic metals into groundwater, and the exemption offers no substitute federal baseline. On balance, the protections foregone outweigh the disposal savings, most of which would accrue to utilities rather than ratepayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to committee, but no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Latta introduced the bill in the House on April 6, 2011 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and then to its Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill sat in committee until the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning utilities came out ahead: the bill died, but so did any chance this Congress would mandate the strictest federal rules for their ash disposal, and the status quo remained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-burning utilities kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to his committee's Environment and the Economy subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor and no organized opposition action on the bill itself [S4].

industries.note: The bill would spare utilities the disposal, lining, and groundwater-monitoring costs of a hazardous-waste designation for coal ash. That saving comes at the expense of communities near ash ponds, who would keep bearing the contamination risk.

industries.industry: Coal ash recyclers (fly ash in concrete and construction materials)
industries.note: A hazardous label can depress demand for recycled fly ash, so exempting it helps the reuse market. Reuse of ash is generally preferable to disposal, though the exemption applies regardless of how the material is handled.
Weaker ash-disposal rules lower the all-in cost of coal-fired generation, indirectly supporting demand for mined coal. The effect is secondary to the bill's direct purposes.
